newsitem.title: UK: Italian bonds storm to first place in week - Salomon. [CORRECTED 10:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Italian bonds storm to first place in week - Salomon. [CORRECTED 10:00 GMT]

text.p: Italian bonds charged to first place among world government bonds this week as enthusiam over European monetary union catapulted all European debt higher, data from Salomon Brothers showed on Friday.
U.S. Treasuries posted gains too, as weak economic data at the beginning of the weak helped dispel lingering worries about the Federal Reserve's steady-as-she-goes interest rate policy.
Overall, the Salomon Brothers world government bond index rose 0.54 percent in local currency terms in the week ended October 3 and 0.23 percent in U.S. dollar terms.
Italian bonds chalked up 1.72 percent gains in lire.

In dollar terms, Italian bonds also led the pack with a stunning 2.12 percent gain, as the lira shined in the face of mark weakness. The dollar jumped to a three-month (Corrects from three-year) high against the mark this week.

With a 1997 budget delivering 62.5 trillion lire in savings on Friday, Italian bonds could do no wrong and there was even talk that Italy could make it into the first wave of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.
Enthusiam over EMU also boosted Italy's high-yielding cousin, Sweden, which posted gains of 1.20 percent in crown terms, putting it second, and 1.68 percent in U.S. dollar terms.
Gains for high-yielding Spain were less specutacular. Bonos advanced 0.66 percent, putting it eighth in Salomon's index in local terms. In dollar terms Bonos made a return of zero.
A 50 basis point cut in Spain's key money market rate to 6.75 percent on Thursday may yet filter through, analysts said.

British gilts, not generally regarded as a contender for the first round of EMU, nevertheless caught EMU fever. Soothing words on the economy from the opposition Labour Party -- at the last party conference before a general election -- also helped.
Gilts advanced 1.10 percent in sterling terms, placing them third in Salomon's table. In dollars, they rose 1.34 percent.

Canadian bonds came fourth in local terms with gains of 1.06 percent as the Bank of Canada cut its overnight rate to 3.50-4.00 percent on Wednesday, revelling in its new-found independence from the U.S. Federal Reserve which held rates steady the week before.
In U.S. dollars, Canadian bonds came third, jumping 1.57 percent.
Next in line in local terms were Danish bonds with 0.83 percent returns, followed closely by Australian bonds which rose 0.80 percent in local terms.
Optimism remains high in the Australian market that third quarter inflation and wage data at the end of October would allow an interest rate cut.

Core European bonds advanced at a steady rate this week in local currency terms, Salomon's index showed. Belgian bonds rose 0.54 percent, French OATs 0.52 percent, Austrian bonds 0.39 perecent, German Bunds 0.33 percent and Dutch bonds 0.21 percent.

But the strength of the dollar resulted in negative returns for these bonds in U.S. terms, with Belgian Olos losing 0.17 percent, OATs 0.10 percent, Austrian bonds 0.19 percent, Bunds 0.26 percent, and guilder bonds 0.35 percent.
The strong dollar was not kind to Japanese bonds in U.S. terms either, putting them last in Salomon's league with losses of 0.71 percent. In yen terms, they managed a 0.27 percent return.

Away from the EMU story, Treasuries gained 0.36 percent amid weak data from the National Association of Purchasing Management. But they faced a tense day on Friday with September non-farm payroll data due at 1230 GMT.

Salomon's bond index is calculated using all government bonds with over one year to maturity, weighted for market capitalisation. Only bonds freely available to institutional investors and with a certain minimum amount outstanding are included. Returns take account of price moves and accrued interest.
